title: Where the JSON Lives
dek: Relational versus non-relational is the wrong first question. The right ones are what shape your reads take, what a lost write costs, and who governs the licence. This is a field guide to both families as they stand in October 2026 — how each stores and finds data, the trade-offs they cannot escape, the licences that changed under people's feet — then a measured answer to a narrower question: if a system loads and stores JSON all day, where should that JSON live, and how do you build it from free, open-source parts that hold up.
byline: 1 October 2026 · Synthesised from project documentation and release notes; write and read costs measured on this machine; the xo-space examples are read from its tree
description: A field guide to relational and non-relational databases, best practices that survive production, and a measured recommendation for storing JSON continuously with free, open-source components.
og_description: Both database families, how they store and find data, the trade-offs they cannot escape, and the 2024–2026 licence changes — then a benchmark of five ways to keep a JSON document current, and a free, open-source stack for loading and storing JSON all day: PostgreSQL 18 JSONB or SQLite in WAL mode, a hybrid schema, Valkey for the hot path, S3-compatible object storage, and ClickHouse or DuckDB for the event history.
twitter_description: Relational vs NoSQL is the wrong first question. A field guide to both, a licence ledger, and a measured answer to where JSON should live.
badges_callout:
How to read the badges

from the docs marks a fact taken from a project's own documentation, release notes, or licence text. from the tree marks something read from the xo-space source, quoted with its path. measured here marks a number produced by _compute.py beside this page, on one 8-CPU Linux machine with Python 3.14 and SQLite 3.46.1 — the ratios travel, the absolute microseconds do not. reconstruction marks a judgement or mechanism I have worked out rather than read. PostgreSQL was not benchmarked here; its behaviour is cited, not measured.

sections.title: The wrong first question
figures: fig-axes · five axes that actually decide (SVG, wide) · data shape, access pattern, consistency need, operational burden, licence/governance — with where 'relational vs NoSQL' sits (it is a proxy for the first axis only)
sections.brief: Thesis: 'SQL vs NoSQL' is a proxy for one of five decisions. JSON is a serialization format, not a database category — every serious relational engine stores it natively now, and every document store has grown schemas and transactions. State the answer up front so a reader can stop here: for a system that loads and stores JSON continuously, the default is PostgreSQL 18 (JSONB, server) or SQLite in WAL mode (embedded, single node), with a hybrid schema — real columns for what you filter, join, or constrain; JSONB for the long tail — plus Valkey for hot ephemeral state, S3-compatible object storage for large blobs, and ClickHouse or DuckDB for analysing the event history. The rest of the page earns that answer. Mention the running example: xo-space today keeps its state as JSON files written via temp file + os.replace, plus JSONL timelines.

sections.title: The relational family
figures: fig-write-path · anatomy of a committed write in PostgreSQL (SVG, wide) · client → WAL record (fsync on commit) → shared buffers → heap page + index → background writer/checkpoint → data file; MVCC tuple versions xmin/xmax; vacuum
sections.brief: What the relational model is (relations, keys, constraints, normalization, declarative queries, planner) and what an engine actually does: WAL-first durability, B-tree indexes, MVCC, isolation levels (read committed default in Postgres; serializable available), vacuum. The open-source members: PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL licence, PGDG; 18 released 25 Sep 2025 with async I/O, uuidv7(), virtual generated columns default; 19 is at Beta 4 on 24 Sep 2026 with RC planned for October — so 18 is the production pick today), MySQL (GPLv2, Oracle) / MariaDB (GPLv2, foundation), SQLite (public domain, embedded, one writer at a time, WAL mode lets readers proceed during a write). Distributed SQL: YugabyteDB and TiDB (Apache 2.0) remain open; CockroachDB retired its free Core edition for a single enterprise licence (late 2024) — not open source. Where relational shines and where it hurts (schema migrations on hot tables, horizontal write scaling, object-relational impedance).

sections.title: The non-relational families
figures: fig-families · eight families, one row each (HTML table or stack rows, wide) · data model, the access pattern it is built for, what it gives up, an open-source pick with licence
fig-shapes · same session record in four models (SVG) · key-value blob, document, wide-column partition/clustering rows, graph nodes/edges
sections.brief: 'NoSQL' is eight different things. Key-value (Valkey 9 BSD-3 under Linux Foundation; Redis 8 back to AGPLv3 since May 2025, tri-licensed; RocksDB/etcd/FoundationDB as building blocks). Document (MongoDB is SSPL — source-available, not OSI open source; CouchDB Apache 2.0 with multi-master replication; FerretDB 2.0 Apache 2.0 speaking the MongoDB wire protocol on top of the DocumentDB PostgreSQL extension, MIT, Linux Foundation since Aug 2025). Wide-column (Apache Cassandra 5, Apache 2.0; ScyllaDB moved to source-available from 2025.1 — last AGPL was 6.2). Graph (Apache AGE on Postgres; Neo4j Community GPLv3). Time-series (TimescaleDB — note its split licence, describe carefully; QuestDB Apache 2.0; VictoriaMetrics Apache 2.0). Search (OpenSearch Apache 2.0; Elasticsearch added AGPL as an option in 2024). Vector (pgvector PostgreSQL licence; Qdrant Apache 2.0). Columnar analytics (ClickHouse Apache 2.0; DuckDB MIT). For each: the access pattern it is built for and what it gives up (joins, ad-hoc queries, strong consistency, or multi-key transactions). Key point: most of these are optimisations of one access pattern; you choose them when that pattern dominates and has outgrown a general engine.

sections.title: The trade-offs nobody escapes
figures: fig-amplification · B-tree vs LSM-tree (SVG, wide) · update-in-place pages vs memtable→SSTables→compaction; read, write, and space amplification arrows
fig-consistency · the consistency ladder (SVG) · eventual → read-your-writes → causal → snapshot → serializable/strict serializable, with which engines default where
sections.brief: Storage engines: B-tree (Postgres heap+btree, InnoDB, SQLite) vs LSM (RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, ClickHouse MergeTree is LSM-like for columns). The RUM conjecture: read, update, memory/space overhead — pick two. Distribution: CAP is about partitions only; PACELC is the useful version (else: latency vs consistency). Consistency models ladder with defaults (Postgres read committed; Cassandra tunable per query with quorum; MongoDB/FerretDB write concern). Replication: single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless. Sharding cost: cross-shard joins and transactions. Concrete rule: a single well-tuned Postgres or even SQLite node handles far more than most products need; distribute when a measured limit forces you, not before. Keep numeric claims sourced or marked reconstruction.

sections.title: Free and open source, checked
figures: fig-ledger · the 2024–2026 licence ledger (HTML table, wide) · project, before, after, date, governance, what it means for self-hosting a SaaS: Redis (BSD→RSALv2/SSPL Mar 2024→+AGPLv3 with Redis 8, May 2025), Valkey (fork, BSD-3, LF), Elasticsearch (SSPL/ELv2 2021→+AGPL Aug 2024), MongoDB (SSPL since 2018), CockroachDB (Core retired, enterprise-only, late 2024), ScyllaDB (AGPL→source-available, Dec 2024/2025.1), MinIO (community edition maintenance mode Dec 2025, repository archived early 2026), NATS (attempted BSL relicense April 2025 blocked; stays Apache 2.0 under CNCF, settled 1 May 2025), DocumentDB (MIT, joined LF Aug 2025)
sections.brief: The user asked for free and open-source. Define it precisely: OSI-approved licence, not 'source-available' (SSPL, BSL, RSAL, ELv2, ScyllaDB's licence). Explain why governance matters more than the licence text today: projects owned by one company relicense; projects held by a foundation (PGDG for Postgres, Apache Software Foundation, Linux Foundation, CNCF) mostly cannot — NATS is the proof case (trademark held by LF blocked the change). AGPL note: fine to run internally and to run behind a network service if you do not modify it, but it does impose obligations if you modify and serve; Garage (AGPLv3) and Redis 8 fall here. Best practice: pin to foundation-governed projects for the system of record; accept single-vendor projects only where swapping is cheap (wire-compatible alternatives exist).

sections.title: Best practices that survive production
figures: fig-expand-contract · expand / migrate / contract for a schema change with two deploy clocks (SVG, wide)
fig-checklist · the operating checklist (stack rows) · design, indexes, migrations, connections, backups, observability, security, retention — one row each with the open-source tool
sections.brief: Concrete, opinionated practices. Design: model the queries first; write them down before the tables. Primary keys: bigint identity or UUIDv7 (time-ordered → B-tree locality; Postgres 18 uuidv7()); never random UUIDv4 as clustered key on hot inserts. Constraints in the database (NOT NULL, CHECK, FK, UNIQUE) are documentation that executes. Indexes: add for a measured query, verify with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS); every index taxes writes. Migrations: expand/contract, never a blocking ALTER on a hot table; use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY; set lock_timeout. Connections: Postgres is process-per-connection — pool with PgBouncer (transaction mode) or the driver pool. Transactions short; no network calls inside. Backups: a backup you have not restored is a hope — pgBackRest or WAL-G for PITR on Postgres, Litestream for SQLite (streams WAL to S3-compatible storage); test restores on a schedule. Observability: pg_stat_statements, auto_explain, slow query log. Security: least-privilege roles, TLS, no superuser app role, row-level security where tenants share tables. Data lifecycle: retention and partitioning for append-only tables (declarative partitioning by time; drop partitions instead of DELETE). Vacuum and bloat: understand autovacuum; avoid long-running transactions. Keep claims cited to docs.

sections.title: What a database does with JSON
figures: fig-jsonb-update · what one changed field costs in PostgreSQL JSONB (SVG, wide) · jsonb_set on a 40 KB document → whole new tuple version → new TOAST chunks (values above ~2 KB TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD are compressed/out-of-line) → WAL volume → old version for vacuum
fig-formats · four on-disk JSON representations (stack rows) · text JSON, PostgreSQL JSONB, SQLite JSONB (3.45+), BSON, ClickHouse JSON (per-path subcolumns)
sections.brief: Text vs binary: Postgres json (text, preserves whitespace/order/dup keys) vs jsonb (decomposed binary, keys sorted and deduplicated, no whitespace, faster to query, slightly slower to write). The critical fact: there is no in-place partial update — jsonb_set produces a new value; MVCC writes a new tuple; large values are TOASTed (compressed with pglz or lz4 via default_toast_compression, out-of-line above ~2 KB), so updating one counter in a 1 MB document rewrites ~1 MB plus WAL. HOT updates only if no indexed column changes and the page has room. Indexes: GIN jsonb_ops (keys + values, supports ?, ?|, ?&, @>) vs jsonb_path_ops (smaller, faster, only @> and jsonpath); B-tree expression indexes on (body->>'status') for equality/range on a known path; generated columns to promote a path. SQL/JSON: jsonpath (PG12+), JSON_TABLE, JSON_EXISTS/JSON_QUERY/JSON_VALUE (PG17). SQLite: JSON functions built in, JSONB binary format since 3.45 (Jan 2024), ->/->> operators, expression indexes, generated columns. MongoDB/FerretDB BSON and the 16 MB document limit. ClickHouse JSON type production-ready in 25.3 — stores each path as a typed subcolumn, so analytics over JSON events is columnar. Rule: keep documents small and stable; anything that grows without bound (logs, messages, events) belongs in rows, not inside one document.

sections.title: Five ways to keep a document current, measured
figures: fig-writes · cost per durable update, log scale (SVG bar chart, wide) · from _numbers.json write section
fig-reads · reads: parse-the-file vs ask-the-database (SVG) · point read and 20k-document filter with and without expression index
sections.brief: Present the benchmark in _numbers.json honestly. Setup: 2,879-byte session document; 1,500 updates each; one 8-CPU Linux machine, Python 3.14.4, SQLite 3.46.1; fsync on a cloud block device. Results (us/op): file tmp+fsync+os.replace 1464.5; same without fsync 241.3; JSONL append fsync each 1153.9; JSONL fsync every 100 lines 14.0; SQLite WAL synchronous=FULL: whole-doc UPDATE 991.0, json_set (text) 411.1, jsonb_set 417.6, event INSERT 412.0, batched 100/tx 8.4; synchronous=NORMAL: whole-doc 34.1, json_set 21.3, jsonb_set 10.8, event INSERT 17.6, batched 3.6. Reads: parse whole file for one field 32.1 us vs SQLite point extract 7.1 us; filter across 20,000 docs on owner+status: 22,061.9 us full scan vs 9.2 us with an expression index (≈2,400×), plan 'SEARCH docs USING INDEX docs_owner_status'. Interpretation: the cost of a durable write is the fsync, not the format; you pay ~0.4–1.5 ms per fsync here, so throughput is set by how many writes share one fsync (batching/group commit). SQLite WAL synchronous=NORMAL does not fsync on each commit — durable across application crash, but the last transactions can roll back on power loss/OS crash (cite SQLite docs). Postgres equivalents: synchronous_commit=off (bounded loss window, ~3×wal_writer_delay, no corruption), commit_delay/group commit. Partial updates beat whole-document rewrites even at equal fsync count because less is written. And a reader that wants one field should not parse the whole file. Caveats: one machine, one doc size, Python overhead included, no concurrency, PostgreSQL not measured. Show the actual _compute.py excerpt for the file-rewrite loop.

sections.title: The hybrid schema
figures: fig-hybrid-row · anatomy of a hybrid row (SVG, wide) · typed columns id/tenant/kind/status/version/updated_at, a JSONB body, a schema_version, generated column promoting a hot path; side table of append-only events; snapshot + events
sections.brief: The pattern to implement. Rule of promotion: a JSON path becomes a column when you filter, sort, join, aggregate, or constrain on it — or when it changes far more often than the rest of the document. Show PostgreSQL DDL (≤25 lines): documents table with id uuid default uuidv7(), tenant_id, kind, status, version int, schema_version smallint, body jsonb NOT NULL with CHECK (jsonb_typeof(body)='object') and a size CHECK (pg_column_size(body) < 64 kB), updated_at; generated column; GIN jsonb_path_ops index; partial B-tree index. Events table partitioned by month. Show an upsert with optimistic concurrency (UPDATE ... SET body = body || $patch, version = version + 1 WHERE id=$1 AND version=$2 RETURNING version) and explain || is shallow merge, jsonb_set for deep paths. Validation in two places: at the edge with Pydantic v2 / JSON Schema (application) and a cheap guard in the database (CHECK constraints; optional pg_jsonschema extension from Supabase, Apache 2.0). schema_version + upgrade-on-read functions (lazy migration). Snapshot + events: hot document stays small; history goes to an append-only table; rebuild a snapshot from events. Show the SQLite equivalent briefly (STRICT table, body BLOB as JSONB, generated column, expression index).

sections.title: A free stack for loading and storing JSON all day
figures: fig-stack · the recommended architecture (SVG, wide) · app (FastAPI/pydantic) → PgBouncer → PostgreSQL 18 (hybrid tables) with pgBackRest → object storage; Valkey for sessions/cache/pubsub/rate limits; large blobs to SeaweedFS/Garage with a pointer row; events table → Debezium or logical replication / NATS JetStream → ClickHouse or DuckDB-over-Parquet; edge colors per house convention (thin blue data, thick black control, dashed purple state)

fig-tiers · three sizes of the same design (tier cards) · single node: SQLite WAL + Litestream; one team server: Postgres 18 + PgBouncer + pgBackRest + Valkey; scale-out: add read replicas, partitioning, CDC to ClickHouse, then Citus or YugabyteDB only if a measured write ceiling forces it
sections.brief: Each component with: what it does in this design, licence, governance, why it over alternatives, and the one configuration that matters. System of record: PostgreSQL 18 (PostgreSQL licence). Embedded/single-process: SQLite in WAL mode + Litestream (Apache 2.0) to S3-compatible storage. MongoDB API needed (existing drivers/tools): FerretDB 2 + DocumentDB extension (Apache 2.0 + MIT) on Postgres — not MongoDB (SSPL). Hot/ephemeral JSON (sessions, presence, rate limits, pub/sub, caches): Valkey 9 (BSD-3, LF; Valkey 9.0 GA 21 Oct 2025) — never the system of record; set maxmemory policy; AOF everysec if you must persist. Large JSON blobs / artefacts (> ~1 MB, write-once): S3-compatible object storage with a pointer row in Postgres; MinIO community edition is in maintenance mode and archived, so SeaweedFS (Apache 2.0) or Garage (AGPLv3, small geo-distributed clusters) or Ceph RGW for big installations. Streams and CDC: NATS JetStream (Apache 2.0, CNCF) for lightweight event fan-out; Apache Kafka 4 if you already run it; Debezium (Apache 2.0) or native logical replication for CDC — use a transactional outbox table instead of dual writes. Analytics on JSON events: ClickHouse (Apache 2.0) with the JSON type (production-ready from 25.3) or DuckDB (MIT) reading Parquet/NDJSON in place. APIs: PostgREST (MIT) if you want HTTP over tables. Python libraries: psycopg 3 (LGPL) or asyncpg (Apache 2.0), orjson or msgspec for fast (de)serialization, Pydantic v2 for validation. Make a clear 'do not' list: don't use Redis/Valkey as the database of record, don't put unbounded arrays in one document, don't store multi-MB blobs in JSONB, don't pick a single-vendor source-available engine for the system of record.

sections.title: Implementing it: from JSON files to tables
figures: fig-migration · moving xo-space off flat files without downtime (SVG, wide) · phases: 1 repository interface over files, 2 dual-write files+DB with DB as shadow, 3 backfill + compare, 4 read from DB, 5 stop writing files; rollback point at each phase
sections.brief: Ground in the xo-space tree. Quote services/cowork_agent/xo_cowork_state.py _atomic_write (lines 53-67: mkstemp in STATE_DIR, json.dump indent=2 sort_keys, flush, os.fsync, os.replace) — the correct way to atomically write a JSON file. Contrast services/xo_manifest.py _write_atomic (lines 133-140: write_text then os.replace with no fsync) — atomic against a crashing process, but after power loss the rename can land before the data; also note neither fsyncs the directory, so the rename itself is not guaranteed durable. Note services/cowork_agent/scopes.py names stats.json, todos.json, timeline.jsonl, sessions/sessionslist.json as a closed set of files the BFF reads, and visualizer.flock for locking. What files do well (inspectable, git-diffable, zero ops) and where they stop (whole-file rewrite per change, one writer via flock, no query without loading everything, no cross-file transaction). Then the implementation: a small repository interface (get, put with expected version, patch, append_event, query) in Python with two backends; show a ~25-line SQLite backend (WAL, synchronous=NORMAL or FULL decision, busy_timeout, jsonb, BEGIN IMMEDIATE for writes) and a ~20-line psycopg 3 / asyncpg Postgres upsert with optimistic concurrency. Migration plan with dual-write and backfill; keep exporting JSON files as a read-only projection if humans or other tools read them. Batching: coalesce high-frequency updates (e.g. usage counters) in memory and flush every N ms in one transaction — the measured section shows why. Be explicit about which parts are recommendation (reconstruction badge).

sections.title: Where this advice stops
sections.brief: Honest limits: multi-region active-active writes with low latency (look at YugabyteDB/TiDB or CRDT-based designs, accept complexity); event volumes in the billions per day (Kafka + ClickHouse as primary, Postgres for metadata); deep graph traversal (a graph engine); relevance-ranked full-text search (OpenSearch alongside, fed by CDC); vectors at hundreds of millions (dedicated engine like Qdrant) — pgvector is fine below that. Also: the benchmark is one machine; Postgres was not measured here; licences change, check the date on this page. End with the one-paragraph decision rule.
